Apple is marking its 50th anniversary this year, and many of its customers are even older than the company itself. It has set up a new support page listing 50 ways to make its devices easier to use, most of which involve accessibility settings.

These tips cover a wide range, from adjusting the text size on an Apple Watch, to getting your iPhone to remind you when the washing machine has finished…

Apple says its goal is to make its technology accessible to everyone, including older users.

At Apple, we believe the best technology should work for everyone, including older adults. That's why inclusion is built into the design of our products and services — through built-in accessibility features that help you connect, create, and do what you love, in ways that work best for you. The way you engage with the world changes as you move through different stages of life. From enlarging onscreen text to making conversations clearer in noisy restaurants, the ecosystem of Apple devices, features, and services is designed to remain flexible to fit your needs.

The support page focuses on accessibility features and is broken down into ten categories.

  • Vision: View your screen more comfortably
  • Hearing: Have conversations, receive alerts, and stay aware of your surroundings
  • Mobility: Adjust how you navigate and control your device
  • Speech: Express yourself the way you prefer
  • Cognitive: Stay focused and in control
  • Personalization: Make the experience your own
  • Organization: Remember what matters
  • Health: Stay informed about your health with helpful information
  • Safety: Enjoy peace of mind
  • Communication: Stay connected

Take the Vision category, for example. It includes features such as enlarging text, bolding text, inverting colors, applying color filters, reducing transparency, increasing contrast, and reducing motion. Some of the features — such as Sound Recognition — were heavily promoted by Apple when they first launched, but remain little-known to this day.

Sound Recognition listens out for specific sounds and uses on-device intelligence to notify you when it detects them. It can recognize 15 different sounds, and you can train the device to recognize your own name and unique electronic sounds in your environment, such as the beeps of kitchen appliances, certain types of alarms, or doorbells. Sound Recognition on the HomePod can even detect the sound of smoke or carbon monoxide alarms. Sound Recognition also works with CarPlay, letting your iPhone pick up and detect sounds such as sirens, car horns, and even a crying baby. When a specific sound is detected, you'll receive a notification — and if you're using CarPlay, the notification will appear on your car's display.

The page is comprehensive, offering a wonderful summary of the many accessibility features currently offered across Apple's devices. Each section offers individual instructions for every supported device, which depending on the feature may include iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, Vision Pro, and CarPlay.
